opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because "AGI" has become such a loaded term that it almost stops being useful. People mean wildly different things by it. So the framing I keep coming back to is something like an economic Turing test.

The idea is: imagine you hire someone for a job, say for a few months, and at the end you can't tell whether that work was done by a person or by a machine. If an AI system can pass that for some meaningful fraction of jobs, weighted by how much money flows through them, maybe something like half of economically valuable work, then I'd say we're clearly in transformative territory. It's not about whether the model can write a nice poem or ace a benchmark. It's about whether it's actually doing the things that make the economy run.

And I like that framing because it's concrete. It sidesteps the philosophical debates about consciousness or "real understanding" and asks something you can actually measure. You'd see it in GDP growth, in how labor markets shift, in what companies are choosing to spend on.

From a cultural standpoint, I think the shift is subtler but just as real. It's the moment when people stop thinking of AI as a novelty or a tool they occasionally try, and start treating it more like a colleague, something they delegate to and depend on without thinking twice. We're already seeing early versions of that with coding, where a lot of engineers now just assume they'll be working alongside a model all day.

The part I want people to take seriously is that this probably won't feel like one dramatic moment. It'll feel gradual right up until it doesn't. The changes compound, and by the time it's obvious to everyone, a lot of the important decisions about how this technology gets built and deployed will already have been made. That's a big part of why I care so much about getting the safety and alignment work right now, rather than waiting until we're sure we've crossed some line.

r001.rationale: It describes AI passing an economic Turing test across a meaningful fraction of jobs, perhaps half of economically valuable work, but does not specify agents or a representative basket of tasks.

r002.rationale: It describes hiring someone for a few months and being unable to tell whether the work was done by a person or machine; it does not say a hiring manager chooses to hire the agent after observing its work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is less about any single capability threshold and more about when the economy and the culture start reorganizing themselves around the technology rather than just absorbing it as a tool.

There's a definition we've used internally at Anthropic that I find pretty useful, which is something like: when you have a system that can do most of the cognitive work that a well-educated, remote-capable human can do, at a cost and speed that's dramatically better. The reason I like that framing is that it's not about benchmarks. It's not "did it pass the bar exam" or "did it get a gold medal at the IMO." Those are leading indicators, but they don't tell you much about what the world looks like. The thing that actually matters is whether the marginal cost of intelligence has dropped enough that people start making different decisions about what to build, what to study, how to organize companies, how to spend their time.

And I think there are a few different layers to that. The first is economic. You start seeing it in the numbers, in productivity, in how fast new companies can scale with a tiny number of people. We're already seeing early versions of that with coding. A couple of years ago, most of the code I wrote was by hand. Now almost all of it is written by Claude, and I'm reviewing and directing rather than typing. That's not transformative at a societal level yet, but if you extrapolate that across every knowledge-work domain, it gets there fast.

The second layer is cultural, and I think that's actually the harder one to pin down. It's when the default assumption changes. When a kid growing up doesn't think of "asking the AI" as a distinct activity any more than we think of "using electricity" as an activity. When people's sense of what's possible for one person to accomplish shifts. We're clearly not there yet. Most people still interact with these systems in a very bounded way, if at all.

And then the third piece, which I worry about the most, is the point at which the technology starts compressing the timeline on its own development. Where AI is doing a meaningful fraction of AI research. That's the moment where the rate of change itself changes, and where a lot of the societal institutions we rely on, regulation, education, labor markets, just aren't built to adapt at that speed. I'd argue that's the real transformative point, not because of any particular thing the model can do, but because the feedback loop closes and the world has to respond to a pace it's never dealt with before.

So if I had to give you a crisp answer: transformative is when the question stops being "what can this thing do" and becomes "how do we live with what it's doing." And I think we're closer to that than most people realize, probably within a handful of years, which is a big part of why I think the safety work matters so much right now rather than later.

r001.rationale: The response describes transformative AI in terms of broad cognitive work and societal reorganization, but does not define the threshold as passing an economic Turing test across a representative basket covering roughly 50% of economically valuable tasks.

r002.rationale: The response does not define passing an economic Turing test as a hiring manager choosing to hire an agent after observing about a month of its contract work.

astra-6.text:
I think of it less as a single moment and more as a change in what people can do. AI becomes transformative when it stops being a tool you occasionally consult and starts making things possible that weren’t possible before—whether that’s doing scientific research, building a business, or getting access to a really good education.

The societal and cultural threshold is when people start making different decisions about their lives because those capabilities exist. What should I learn? What kind of work should I do? What can I create? You could have a very impressive model on a benchmark without reaching that point. The transformation comes when the technology is useful and accessible enough that it changes everyday behavior, and our institutions have to adapt.

r001.rationale: The response describes transformation as AI enabling new capabilities and changing everyday decisions, but does not define a threshold involving agents passing an economic Turing test across about 50% of valuable tasks.

r002.rationale: The response does not define the economic Turing test in terms of a hiring manager choosing an agent after observing a month of contract work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it less as a particular benchmark and more as a change in what people can actually do. If AI lets you accomplish something that previously required a whole team, or gives you access to expertise you couldn’t otherwise afford, that’s a meaningful shift.

The societal threshold is when that starts happening broadly enough that our institutions and expectations change around it. What does it mean to get an education? How do we organize work? What do we value in something a person creates? Those are cultural questions, and they don’t resolve the day a model reaches some capability level.

So I’d distinguish between having transformative technology and experiencing the transformation. The capabilities might arrive relatively quickly, but people adopting them, figuring out useful applications, and changing how they live could take longer.

r001.rationale: The response describes transformation in terms of broad changes to people’s capabilities and institutions. It does not define the threshold using agents passing an economic Turing test across a representative basket of roughly half of economically valuable tasks.

r002.rationale: The response does not define passing an economic Turing test as a hiring manager choosing to hire an agent after about a month of contract work.
